extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, historians, and observers of American institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and explicate the principal social, institutional, geographic, and moral factors that promote or threaten the maintenance of a democratic republic (with emphasis on the United States, 19th-century perspective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of external threats (no neighbors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Americans have no neighbors, and consequently they have no great wars, or financial crises, or inroads, or conquest to dread; they require neither great taxes, nor great armies, nor great generals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because foreign threats are minimal, the U.S. does not develop large standing armies or suffer the distortions that military competition imposes on republican institutions; this physical/political situation is counted among the chief causes favoring democratic stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of military glory to republics
rubrics_metrics.description: A scourge more formidable to republics than wars or taxes is military glory; military reputations can elevate unqualified leaders (example: General Jackson) and carry the people away by illusions of glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a polity's admiration of military success enables mediocre or authoritarian leaders to assume disproportionate power; rarity of battles amplifies the cult of military fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a dominant national metropolis
rubrics_metrics.description: America has no great capital — a city whose influence is directly or indirectly felt over the whole extent of the country — which is one of the first causes of the maintenance of republican institutions in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single dominant metropolis concentrates influence and can endanger representative systems by enabling a populace to affect national policy in ways that are dangerous to republicanism; dispersion of influence across many cities is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perils of large urban populations and their composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Large American cities contain lower orders constituting a rabble (freed blacks, European emigrants without civil rights) who may inoculate the country with vices and are ready to turn communal passions to their advantage, producing riots and local corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess urban populations for social composition, levels of local corruption, and the capacity of city populace to exert unchecked influence; such conditions are a real danger to democratic republics unless checked by other institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cities acting as assemblies and threat to representative system
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities may be looked upon as large assemblies; their populace exercises a prodigious influence upon the magistrates, and frequently executes its own wishes without their intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how concentrated urban popular power can bypass institutional checks and destabilize representative governance; municipal majorities can impose policies detrimental to broader republican stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for an armed force independent of town populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Prediction that republics will perish unless the government creates an armed force which, whilst it remains under the control of the majority of the nation, will be independent of the town population, and able to repress its excesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether national coercive forces are insulated from local urban mobs yet remain accountable to the national majority—a safeguard against urban insurrections undermining republican order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and character of early settlers (equality of conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The origin of the American settlements — the equal chances of birth and the customs, manners, and opinions bequeathed by forefathers — is the first and most efficacious cause of present prosperity and the rise of democratic republics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine historical patterns of settlement and inherited social norms that favor equality of conditions; such cultural legacies promote republican institutions by shaping citizens' dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial abundance (boundless continent) enabling equality and freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: God himself gave them the means of remaining equal and free, by placing them upon a boundless continent, which is open to their exertions; physical causes independent of laws promote general prosperity and thereby support democratic constitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess geographic/resource endowments and their role in enabling mobility, property acquisition, and broad prosperity that mitigate pressures toward revolution or oligarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous emigration and westward expansion as stabilizing forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuous removal of the human race westward prevents overpopulation of older states, provides opportunities for advancement, reduces division of estates, and fosters social mobility (examples: Connecticut supplying many representatives to new western states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider population mobility and frontier opportunities as mechanisms preventing concentrated poverty and class stagnation, thereby preserving democratic equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property laws plus frontier conditions prevent excessive parcelling of estates
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of the United States are extremely favorable to the division of property; but the abundance of land and continual emigration prevent property from being divided to excess, re-establishing practical primogeniture without legal compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how legal rules interact with economic opportunity (availability of land) to shape inheritance practices and social structure; the frontier offsets legal tendencies that might fragment holdings to unsustainable levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restless pursuit of fortune and commercial passions as civic stabilizers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Americans' rapacity for securing fortune, restlessness, excessive love of independence, and commercial passions — though seen as vices in Europe — ensure a long and peaceful duration to the republics of America by dispersing population and promoting industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze cultural proclivities toward enterprise and mobility: traits that in this context channel ambitions into lawful economic activity rather than revolution, thus supporting republican stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical, order-loving temperament (business habits in politics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans introduce business habits into political life: they love order, value regular conduct and good sense which amasses fortunes, prefer practice to theory, and are more alarmed by general ideas than by practical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether civic culture privileges procedural order, pragmatism, and calculative thinking — characteristics that temper radical political experimentation and support stable governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal form of government combining large power with small-state security
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal form of Government enables the Union to combine the power of a great empire with the security of a small State and is one of the principal causes contributing to the maintenance of the democratic republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate constitutional arrangements for their capacity to balance central authority and local autonomy so as to harness resources while protecting local liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal institutions limiting majority despotism and teaching freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal institutions limit the despotism of the majority, and at the same time impart a taste for freedom and a knowledge of the art of being free to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the strength and distribution of local self-government: robust municipal institutions serve both as brakes on national majoritarian excesses and as schools of civic freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution of the judicial power as check on democratic excesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts of justice serve to repress the excesses of democracy, and to check and direct the impulses of the majority without stopping its activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess judicial independence, scope, and norms: a well-constituted judiciary moderates majority impulses while allowing democratic processes to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners (mores) including intellectual and moral condition support republic
rubrics_metrics.description: The manners of the people — comprising notions, opinions, moral and intellectual condition — are a general cause to which the maintenance of a democratic republic is attributable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prevailing civic morals, shared opinions, and intellectual habits that shape citizens' readiness for democratic self-government; manners operate as cultural infrastructure for institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as a political institution supporting democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every religion is to be found in juxtaposition to a political opinion; most of British America was peopled by men who brought a democratic and republican Christianity which contributed powerfully to the establishment of a democracy and a republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how dominant religious traditions align with political norms: when religion inculcates duties toward others and equality of believers, it buttresses democratic values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catholicism's unexpected affinity with democratic equality (in U.S. context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary to expectation, Catholicism in the United States constitutes one of the most republican and democratic classes of citizens because the Church's internal equality (priest vs people) and the Catholics' social position (mostly poor, a minority) incline them to favor equal political rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how a religious group's internal structure and socio-economic position condition its political stances; minority and poorer groups may favor universal rights irrespective of doctrinal hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of clergy from government produces Catholic support for equality
rubrics_metrics.description: If the priesthood is entirely separated from the government, as in the United States, then no class is more naturally disposed than the Catholics to transfuse the doctrine of the equality of conditions into the political world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional church-state separation: when clergy are not integrated with state power, religious communities may adopt egalitarian political positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect influence of religious morality across sects on social stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Although sects differ in worship, they agree in duties owed from man to man; Christian morality common to all sects influences manners — respect for marriage, limits imagination, checks passion for innovation — thereby contributing substantially to the maintenance of the democratic republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether shared moral norms across diverse religious sects produce common civic virtues that restrain destabilizing impulses and support orderly political life.
